questions.question:
Which of the following statements is correct regarding the production possibility frontier?

I. It gives the combinations between two goods that can be produced when the resources of the economy are fully utilised.

II. It illustrates the production possibilities of the economy.
questions.solution:
Correct Answer **Both I and II**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__****Production Possibility Frontier (PPF):**

**Statement 1:**

 
• The **PPF** does indeed illustrate the combinations of **two goods or services** that can be produced when the resources of the economy are **fully and efficiently utilized.**
 
• It shows the trade-off between the production of **one good and the production of another, **assuming all resources are used to their **fullest potential.**

**Statement 2:**

 
• The PPF also illustrates the **production possibilities of the economy.**
 
• It shows the maximum possible output combinations of two goods or services an economy can achieve when all resources are **fully and efficiently employed.**
 
• The **PPF **is typically depicted as a downward-sloping curve, with **one good on each axis.**
 
• Points along the curve represent efficient production levels, while points below the curve indicate **inefficiency **and points above the curve are unattainable with current resources and technology.

questions.question: In the context of microfinance, what does ‘S’ stand for in SHG?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Self**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Self-Help Groups (SHGs)** are informal associations of people who choose to come together to find ways to improve their living conditions.
 
• They are usually composed of 10-20 members, often women, from similar socio-economic backgrounds.
 
• The primary objective of SHGs is to enhance the socio-economic conditions of their members through collective efforts and mutual support.
 
• SHGs play a crucial role in financial inclusion by enabling members to pool their savings, access credit, and engage in income-generating activities.
 
• SHGs are a key component of microfinance initiatives, providing a platform for the delivery of financial services to the underserved and marginalized sections of society.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Microfinance**

 
 
• Microfinance refers to the provision of financial services to low-income individuals or groups who typically lack access to traditional banking services.
 
• It includes a range of services such as microcredit, savings, insurance, and remittances.
 
• Microfinance aims to promote financial inclusion and empower economically disadvantaged people.
 
• It has been recognized as a powerful tool for poverty alleviation and socio-economic development.
 
 
 
• **Financial Inclusion**
 
 
• Financial inclusion involves ensuring that individuals and businesses have access to useful and affordable financial products and services.
 
• These services should meet their needs and be delivered responsibly and sustainably.
 
• Financial inclusion is essential for reducing poverty, fostering economic growth, and promoting social equity.
 
 
 
• **Women Empowerment through SHGs**
 
 
• SHGs have been instrumental in empowering women by enhancing their financial independence and decision-making power.
 
• Participation in SHGs helps women develop skills, confidence, and a sense of solidarity.
 
• Empowered women contribute to the well-being of their families and communities, leading to broader social and economic development.
 
 
 
• **Government Support for SHGs**
 
 
• The Indian government, through various schemes and programs, supports the formation and strengthening of SHGs.
 
• Initiatives like the National Rural Livelihood Mission (NRLM) aim to promote SHGs and enhance their capacity.
 
• Government support includes financial assistance, training, and capacity-building activities for SHG members.

questions.question: GDP calculated at some constant set of prices is called ______.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**real GDP.**__ [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Real GDP** is calculated by **adjusting nominal GDP **for** inflation**, which gives a more accurate measure of **economic growth.**
 
• Real GDP is used to compare** economic growth over time**, as it reflects changes in the quantity of **goods and services **produced rather than changes in prices.
 
• **Domestic GDP** is a measure of the value of all goods and services produced within a **country's borders,** regardless of the nationality of the producers.
 
• **Current GDP** refers to the most recent measurement of a** country's GDP,** regardless of the prices used to calculate it.
 
• **Nominal GDP** is calculated using **current prices** and does not account for **inflation, **which can lead to an overestimation of economic growth.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **GDP** stands for **Gross Domestic Product** and is a measure of the **total value of goods and services **produced within a country's borders.
 
• **Real GDP** is considered a more accurate measure of economic growth because it adjusts for inflation, which can distort the** value of goods and services produced.**
 
• **Domestic GDP** is often used in conjunction with other measures, such as **Gross National Product (GNP)**, which includes the value of goods and services produced by a country's citizens, regardless of where they are located.
 
• **Current GDP **is useful for** tracking short-term changes **in the economy, but it may not provide an accurate picture of long-term trends.
 
• **Nominal GDP** is often used to compare the** economic size of different countries or regions**, but it can be misleading if prices are not taken into account.

questions.question: Which of the following expression is correct?

options.text: Gross primary deficit = Gross fiscal deficit + Net interest liabilities
Gross primary deficit = Gross fiscal deficit – Net interest liabilities
Gross primary deficit = Gross fiscal deficit ÷ Net interest liabilities
Gross primary deficit = Gross fiscal deficit × Net interest liabilities

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Gross primary deficit = Gross fiscal deficit – Net interest liabilities**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Gross Primary Deficit is the Gross Fiscal Deficit less interest payments.
 
• Net Primary Deficit is Net Fiscal Deficit minus net interest payments.
 
• Fiscal deficit indicates total government borrowing requirements including interest whereas primary deficit indicates total government borrowing requirements excluding interest payments.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__** 

 
• The deficit is the amount by which the spending done in a budget surpasses the earnings. 
 
• There are three types of deficit:

 
• Revenue deficit
 
• Fiscal deficit
 
• Primary deficit. 

 
• Revenue deficit:

 
 
• A revenue deficit refers to the surplus of the government’s revenue expenditure over the revenue receipts.
 
• It reflects the inefficiency of the government to reach its regular or recurring expenditure.
 
• The government may raise its revenue receipts by raising income tax.
 
• Revenue deficit = Revenue expenditure – Revenue receipts
 
 
 
• Fiscal deficit:
 
 
• A fiscal deficit is the excess of budget expenditure over budget receipts other than borrowings.
 
• It reflects the total government borrowings during a fiscal year.
 
• Gross fiscal deficit = Total expenditure – (Revenue receipts + Non-debt creating capital receipts)
 
• Gross fiscal deficit = Net borrowing at home + Borrowing from RBI + Borrowing from abroad
 
 
 
• ​Primary deficit:
 
 
• The purpose of measuring the primary deficit is to draw attention to current fiscal imbalances
 
• The primary deficit is calculated in order to obtain an estimate of the amount of borrowing that will be required due to current expenditures exceeding revenues.
 
• Gross primary deficit = Gross fiscal deficit – Net interest liabilities

questions.question: Which Indian state recorded the highest GST revenue collection for December 2019?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Maharashtra**__.

__
 
• The Gross GST (Goods and Services Tax) revenue collection for December 2019 has crossed the Rs 1 lakh crore mark, showing a growth of 16 per cent in revenue. 
 
 
• **State-wise, Maharashtra recorded the highest GST collection for December at Rs 16,530 crore, followed by Karnataka (Rs 6,886 crore) and Tamil Nadu (Rs 6,422 crore)**__.
 
• In November, GST revenue stood at Rs 1.03 lakh crore, showing a growth of 9 per cent.
 
• The gross GST revenue collected in October was Rs 95,380 crore.
 
• It was Rs 91,916 crore in September, while the tax collection in August was Rs 98,202 crore.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

 
• The** Goods and Services Tax (GST)** is an indirect tax (or consumption tax) used on the supply of goods and services in India.

 
 
• It is a comprehensive, multilevel, destination-based tax: comprehensive because it includes almost all indirect taxes except some state taxes.
 
• In India, the GST Bill was first introduced as the Constitution **(122nd Amendment) Bill in 2014**.
 
• **It was approved in 2016 and re-designated by Rajya Sabha as the Constitution (101st Amendment) Act, 2016**.
 
• **Article 246A **- States have the right to levy taxes on goods and services.
 
• On **1st July 2017**, GST to be applicable across India.

questions.question: What is the most generally used indicator of overall economic performance?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Per capita Gross National Product**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Per capita Gross National Product** is the most generally used indicator of **overall economic performance**.
 
• Per capita Gross National Product (GNP) is indeed a widely used indicator to gauge the economic performance of a country.
 
• It measures the average economic output per person in a given country, providing insight into the standard of living and economic well-being of its citizens.
 
• By dividing the total GNP of a country by its population, policymakers, economists, and analysts can assess trends in economic growth, compare the economic performance of different countries, and make informed decisions regarding economic policies and strategies.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **The Human Development Index (HDI)** indeed serves as a comprehensive measure of a country's social and economic development, encompassing key factors like education, health, and income. By combining indicators such as mean years of schooling, expected years of schooling, life expectancy at birth, and gross national income (GNI) per capita, the HDI provides a holistic assessment of human well-being and development across different nations.
 
• **The Physical Quality of Life Index (PQLI)** offers another perspective on societal well-being by considering various social factors, including life expectancy, infant mortality rate, and literacy rate. It provides a broader understanding of the overall quality of life within a population, highlighting areas for improvement and policy intervention.
 
• **The standard of living** refers to the overall level of prosperity and well-being enjoyed by individuals or communities, typically measured by factors such as income, access to basic needs, and quality of life indicators. It provides insight into the material comforts, services, and opportunities available to people within a given society or location, reflecting their economic and social status.

questions.question: In India, a Small-scale industry is defined with reference to the ______.

options.text: Maximum investment allowed on the assets of a unit.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Maximum investment allowed on the assets of a unit**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• In India, small-scale industries, or **Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs), **are defined by how much money is invested in the business's equipment or machinery.
 
• This is the main way they are classified.
 
• Other factors like the **number of directors, partners, or employees** are not used to define these businesses.
 
• **Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) **are a **crucial part of the economic fabric of many countries, including India. ​**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Classification:** The categories are as follows:
 
• **Micro:** For the manufacturing sector, investment in plant and machinery should not exceed INR 1 crore, and annual turnover should not exceed INR 5 crores.
 
• **Small:** For the manufacturing sector, investment in plant and machinery should be more than INR 1 crore but not exceed INR 10 crores, and annual turnover should not exceed INR 50 crores. 
 
• **Medium: **For the manufacturing sector, investment in plant and machinery should be more than INR 10 crores but not exceed INR 50 crores, and annual turnover should not exceed INR 250 crores.

questions.question:
Which of the following statements is correct regarding the socialist society in the economy?

I. The government decides what goods are to be produced.

II. Distribution of goods under socialism is supposed to be based on what people need.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Both I and II**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **In a socialist society or economy:**

 
 
• The government decides what goods are to be produced.
 
• **Central planning and public ownership of the means of production play** a significant role in determining what goods and services are produced and in what quantities.
 
• The distribution of **goods under socialism is supposed to be based on what people need.**
 
• The aim is to ensure that** everyone's basic needs are met, promoting a more equitable distribution of wealth and reducing income inequality.**
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
 

 Aspect
 Socialist Economy
 Capitalist Economy
 
 
 
 

 Ownership of Means of Production
 Owned and controlled by the state or workers' cooperatives
 Owned and controlled by private individuals or corporations
 
 

 Price Mechanism
 Absent or limited use of market pricing mechanisms
 The central role of market pricing mechanisms in determining prices
 
 

 Distribution of Resources
 Decided by the state or a central planning authority
 Decided by the market forces of supply and demand
 
 

 Economic Inequality
 Strives for economic equality and a more even distribution of resources
 Tolerates economic inequality and rewards individual effort and success
 
 

 Role of Government
 Plays a large role in the economy, regulating and managing the means of production
 Limited role in the economy, primarily enforcing laws and contracts
 
 

 Social Services
 Universal access to healthcare, education, and social services
 Access to healthcare, education, and social services is determined by an individual's ability to pay
 
 

 Innovation and Creativity
 Emphasis on collective innovation and public goods
 Emphasis on individual innovation and private property rights
 
 

 Competition
 Limited competition or controlled competition between state-owned enterprises
 Emphasis on free market competition between private businesses
 
 

 Motivation
 Motivated by the collective good and contributing to society
 Motivated by individual gain and profit
 
 

 Efficiency
 May suffer from inefficiencies due to central planning or lack of competition
 Emphasis on efficiency through market competition and profit incentives

questions.question: Which of the following is defined as 'the point where supply equals demand for a product with equilibrium price'?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Market Equilibrium.**__

__** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] Key Points__**

__
 
• **Market Equilibrium** is defined as 'the point where supply equals demand for a product with equilibrium price'.
 
• The equilibrium price is the price of a good or service when the supply of it is equal to the demand for it in the market.
 
• Thus the market equilibrium for a commodity is determined by balancing the forces of demand and supply for the commodity.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The **demand curve** for unitary elastic demand is a rectangular hyperbola.

 
 
• When the proportionate change in demand produces the same change in the price of the product the demand is referred to as unitary elastic demand.
 
• The **elasticity of a unitary elastic demand is 1.**
 
 
 
• **The supply curve is the positive relationship between the quantity supplied of goods and their price, keeping other factors constant.**
 
 
• Whenever there is a change in the price of goods, there is a movement along the supply curve. due to a change in the supply of goods.

questions.question: Recreation services are an example of ______.
questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**consumer goods**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Recreation services** fall under the category of **consumer goods** as they are directly used by individuals for personal satisfaction and enjoyment.
 
• **Consumer goods** are products that are purchased for consumption by the average consumer.
 
• These goods can be categorized into **durable goods** (such as cars and furniture) and **non-durable goods** (such as food and clothing).
 
• Recreation services, such as amusement parks, theatres, and sports events, provide entertainment and leisure activities to consumers, fulfilling their **recreational needs**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **capital goods**__

 __
 
• **Capital goods** are goods used in the production of other goods or services. These include machinery, buildings, and equipment.
 
• They are not directly consumed by consumers but are used to create products that are then sold to consumers.
 
 
 
• **intermediate goods**__
 __
 
• **Intermediate goods** are products that are used in the production process to produce other goods. They are not final goods and are typically used to produce consumer or capital goods.
 
• Examples include raw materials like steel, wood, and components like microchips.
 
 
 
• **inferior goods**__
 
 
• **Inferior goods** are goods for which demand decreases as the income of consumers increases. These goods are typically lower-cost alternatives to more expensive goods.
 
• Examples include generic brands and off-brand grocery items.

questions.question: Based on the recommendation of the Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices, the Minimum Support Price (MSP) in India is declared by ______,
questions.solution:
The correct answer is ​**Government of India.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Based on the recommendations of the Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices (CACP),** the Department of Agriculture and Co-operation and Farmers Welfare, Government of India, declares Minimum Support Price (MSP) for 23 crops before the sowing season**. 
 
• The** idea behind MSP is to give guaranteed price and assured market to the farmers** and protect them from the price fluctuations and market imperfections. The guaranteed price and assured market are **expected to encourage higher investment and in adoption of modern farming practices**. Further, with the globalization resulting in freer trade in agricultural commodities, it is very important to protect the farmers and their interest.
 
• The evaluation study on MSP was carried out by the erstwhile Programme Evaluation Organization (PEO), now the Development Monitoring and Evaluation Office(DMEO), on a request received from the Ministry of Agriculture, Government of India.
 
• The study was designed with an objective to explore the effectiveness of MSP and to ascertain if the intended benefits have reached the farmers after such a long period of implementation. 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The** Commission for Agricultural Costs & Prices (CACP) is an attached office of the Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare**, Government of India.

 
 
• It came into existence in January 1965.
 
• Currently, the Commission comprises a Chairman, Member Secretary, one Member (Official) and two Members (Non-Official).
 
• The non-official members are representatives of the farming community and usually have an active association with the farming community. 
 
• The Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs headed by the Prime Minister announces the MSP twice in a limited year, once for Kharif crop and once for Rabi crop.

__

• **Capital Expenditure **refers to the expenditure incurred on acquiring or improving fixed assets such as **land, buildings, machinery, **etc.

questions.question: ______ refers to money that has already been spent and which cannot be recovered.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Sunk cost.**__

__
 
• A** sunk cost** refers to** money** that has **already been spent **and which** cannot be recovered**.** Sunk costs** are those which have **already been incurred **and which are **unrecoverable. **
 
• For example, a** manufacturing firm **may have a number of **sunk costs**, such as the **cost of machinery, equipment, and the lease expense on the factory.**
 
• In business,** sunk costs are typically not included in consideration when making future decisions**, as they are seen as irrelevant to current and future budgetary concerns.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Imputed cost or opportunity cost** is the** cost incurred **during the period when **an asset is employed for a particular use, rather than redirecting the asset to a different use.** This amount is the incremental difference between the two options. 
 
• The** imputed cost **can be understood from the following example- suppose a company has a pile of **cash **that earns only **150 basis points** or** 1.5 per cent** in a money market account. Meanwhile,** alternative** risk-free securities are** yielding 2%.** The imputed cost is **50 basis points or 0.5 per cent**, the foregone amount that** the company would be earning if it invested the cash in the higher-yielding securities.**
 
• **Replacement cost **is a term referring to the **amount of money a business must currently spend to replace an essential asset** like a real estate property, investment security, or another item, **with one of the same or higher value**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Privatisation involves the transfer of ownership or management from the public sector (government) to the private sector.
 
• This process is aimed at increasing efficiency and profitability by leveraging private sector management practices and investment.
 
• Privatisation can take various forms, including the sale of government-owned enterprises, public-private partnerships (PPPs), and outsourcing of services.
 
• It is often part of broader economic reforms to stimulate competition, attract foreign investment, and reduce the fiscal burden on the government.

• **Public Sector:**

• **Private Sector:**
 
 
• Consists of businesses and enterprises that are owned and operated by private individuals or companies.
 
• The primary goal of private sector entities is to generate profit and they operate under competitive market conditions.
 
 
 
• **Public-Private Partnership (PPP):**
 
 
• A collaborative arrangement between government and private sector entities to undertake projects or provide services.
 
• PPPs leverage the efficiency and expertise of the private sector while ensuring that public objectives are met.
 
 
 
• **Economic Reforms:**
 
 
• Policies and measures implemented by a government to improve the economic performance and efficiency of a country.
 
• Reforms often include deregulation, liberalization, privatization, and measures to enhance competition and attract investment.

questions.question: Which of the following is **NOT** a central economic problem, which is solved by the production possibility curve (PPC)?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Continuous use.**__

__
 
• A **production possibilities curve (PPC)** shows the maximum amount of one good that can be produced given a production level for some other good, and given the total amounts of inputs available for the production of both goods, and given the technology of production. 
 
• The PPC can be used to illustrate the concepts of **scarcity, opportunity cost, Economic efficiency, inefficiency, economic growth and development, and contractions.**

** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] Additional Information__**

 
• The Production Possibilities Curve (PPC) is a model that captures scarcity and the opportunity costs of choices when faced with the possibility of producing two goods or services.
 
• The **production possibility ****curve** represents graphically alternative production possibilities open to an economy.
 
• The productive resources of the community can be used for the production of various alternative goods.
 
• In other words, the **production possibility curve** can be defined as a graph that represents different combinations of quantities of two goods that can be produced by an economy under the condition of limited available resources. It is also known as the** production possibility frontier(PPFs) or transformation curve.**
 
• The PPCs are normally drawn as bulging upwards or outwards from the origin ("concave" when viewed from the origin), but they can be represented as bulging downward (inwards) or linear (straight), depending on a number of assumptions.
 
• In this diagram AF is the production possibility curve, also called or the production possibility frontier, which shows the various combinations of the two goods (Wheat & Cloth) which the economy can produce with a given amount of resources.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/8468d5c8224748423271b55e9386ce5929013e43f1502f8f581a99c99a5d96b0.png] 

 
• The **Curve** shows all of the possible combinations of 2 goods or services that can be produced within a specified time with all its resources fully and efficiently employed.
 
• The **economy** can produce at any combination on or inside the curve (C and H).
 
• Point outside the curve is not attainable (F).

questions.question: Which of the following is referred to as a relaxation of Government restrictions?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Liberalisation **__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__ **

__
 
• **Liberalisation:**

 
 
• Liberalisation refers to the relaxation of government restrictions, particularly in economic policies.
 
• It involves reducing barriers to trade, deregulating industries, and encouraging private sector participation.
 
• The goal is to promote economic growth, increase efficiency, and attract foreign investment.
 
• In India, economic liberalisation began in 1991, marking a shift from a controlled economy to a market-oriented one.
 
• Key reforms included reducing import tariffs, abolishing industrial licensing, and opening up sectors to foreign investment.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Disinvestment:**

 
 
• Disinvestment refers to the sale or liquidation of government-owned assets or stakes in public sector enterprises.
 
• It is a strategy to reduce the government's role in the economy and raise funds for other priorities.
 
• Disinvestment can lead to increased efficiency and better management of privatized entities.
 
• However, it can also result in job losses and reduced control over strategic sectors.
 
• In India, disinvestment has been used to reform public sector undertakings (PSUs) and reduce fiscal deficits.
 
 
 
• **Globalisation:**
 
 
• Globalisation refers to the integration of economies, cultures, and societies through trade, investment, and technology.
 
• It involves the free flow of goods, services, capital, and information across borders.
 
• Globalisation has led to increased economic interdependence and opportunities for growth.
 
• However, it also raises concerns about inequality, cultural homogenization, and environmental degradation.
 
• In India, globalisation has been a key driver of economic reforms since 1991.
 
• **Privatisation:**
 
 
• Privatisation involves transferring ownership of government-owned enterprises to private entities.
 
• It aims to improve efficiency, reduce government debt, and promote competition.
 
• Privatisation can lead to better management and innovation in previously state-run industries.
 
• However, it can also result in reduced access to essential services and job losses.
 
• In India, privatisation has been part of economic reforms to enhance productivity and attract private investment.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an example of small savings?

• **Small savings instruments,** on the other hand, are financial tools designed to help individuals achieve their financial goals over a specific period.
 
• These instruments include popular options such as the Public Provident Fund (PPF), Sukanya Samriddhi Scheme, Senior Citizen Savings Scheme, Post Office Savings Account, 5-Year Post Office Recurring Deposit Account (RD), and National Savings Certificates (NSC).

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **The National Savings Certificate (NSC)** is a government-backed savings bond in India that forms a part of the postal savings system. It offers a fixed interest rate and is considered a safe investment option for individuals.
 
• **Kisan Vikas Patra (KVP)** is a saving certificate scheme introduced by India Post in 1988. It aims to encourage long-term savings among small investors. KVPs have a fixed maturity period and offer guaranteed returns.
 
• **Post office deposits,** also known as Post-Office Term Deposits (POTDs) or National Savings Time Deposit Accounts, are investment savings accounts offered by India Post. These accounts allow individuals to deposit a lump sum for a fixed period and earn a predetermined rate of interest. They provide a secure way to save money for the future.

questions.question:
Read the following about Capital receipts.

A. All those receipts of the government which create liability or reduce financial assets are termed as capital receipts.

B. The main items of capital receipts are loans raised by the government from the public which are called market borrowings, borrowing by the government from the Reserve Bank and commercial banks and other financial institutions through the sale of treasury bills, loans received from foreign governments and international organisations, and recoveries of loans granted by the central government.

Identify the CORRECT statement/statements.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Both A and B**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Capital receipts** include all receipts that either create a liability or reduce assets.
 
• They are essential for financing the fiscal deficit of the government.
 
• Examples of capital receipts are loans raised by the government, borrowings from the Reserve Bank, and recoveries of loans granted by the central government.
 
• Capital receipts are different from revenue receipts which do not create liabilities or reduce financial assets.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Capital Receipts**

 
 
• Loans raised by the government: These include market borrowings, bonds, and loans from financial institutions.
 
• Borrowings from the Reserve Bank: This includes short-term and long-term borrowings.
 
• Loans from foreign governments and international organizations: These are usually obtained for specific projects or economic support.
 
• Recoveries of loans: These are repayments of loans previously granted by the government to states, public sector enterprises, or other entities.
 
 
 
• **Revenue Receipts**
 
 
• Unlike capital receipts, revenue receipts do not create any liabilities or reduce financial assets.
 
• Examples include tax revenues (income tax, corporate tax, GST) and non-tax revenues (interest receipts, dividends, fees).
 
 
 
• **Fiscal Deficit**
 
 
• The fiscal deficit is the difference between the government's total expenditure and its total receipts (excluding borrowings).
 
• Capital receipts are often used to bridge the fiscal deficit gap.

• Department of Economic Affairs under the Ministry of Finance has been entrusted with the responsibility of preparation and presentation of the Union Budget to Parliament.
 
• It formulates and monitors the country's economic policies and programs having a bearing on domestic and international aspects of economic management.
 
 
• Headquarters - New Delhi
 
• Ministry - Ministry of Finance
 
• Finance Minister - Smt. Nirmala Sitharaman (As of July 2022)
 
 
 
• The Union Budget is also referred to as the Annual Financial Statement in Article 112 of the Constitution of India.
 
• It is the annual budget of the Republic of India.

questions.question: Among the following, which of these are an example of capital receipt?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Borrowings and loan recovery.**__ [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Capital receipt** refers to the** inflow of funds** that do not result from the** regular business operations** of a company.
 
• **Borrowings** and** loan recovery** are examples of **capital receipts** because they involve the** inflow of funds** that are not generated from the company's regular business activities.
 
• **Borrowings** refer to the funds borrowed by a company from **external sources** such as **banks or financial institutions.**
 
• **Loan recovery **refers to the **repayment of loans** that were previously taken by the company.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Rent and commission received, sale of goods and rent, and commission and dividend received are not examples of capital receipt because they are generated from the** regular business operations** of a company.
 
• **Rent and commission** received are** revenues earned by a company** for providing services or renting out property.
 
• **Sale of goods** and rent refers to the sale of goods and the** rental income earned from that sale.**
 
• **Commission and dividend** received are payments made to a company for services rendered or as a **return on investment in shares.**
